pitfalls: Too few trained family therapists → audit the offer, not delivery; report waiting time separately.
Family work is recorded in a separate psychology system → check both systems.
The service user refuses family involvement → record and exclude.
The field is ticked without a real offer → ask for the offer date and who made it.
pearls: Recruit the team psychologist and a family work-trained care coordinator.
Agree a standard family intervention leaflet to hand over at the offer.
Link the field to the carer assessment offer so both happen at one visit.
Hand quarterly reporting to the team manager.

pitfalls: No ward psychologist → a referral to the community team counts; agree this before cycle 1.
Short, chaotic admissions → exclude stays under 7 days.
Psychology notes kept separately → include them in the search.
Offers without capacity to deliver → report waiting lists to the psychological therapies lead.
pearls: Recruit the ward psychologist as co-lead.
Keep the discharge summary line short with fixed options.
Link with the family intervention audit so both are offered together.
Ask the discharge coordinator to check the line.

pitfalls: Few new starts in one team → pool community, crisis and early intervention teams.
Reviews done by care coordinators are not always recorded as medication reviews → accept any contact that asks about side effects and mood.
Start date unclear → use the date of the first prescription.
GP-started antidepressants muddy the sample → include only team-started prescriptions.
pearls: Recruit a team pharmacist to pull new antidepressant starts.
Agree that a telephone call counts.
Put the 7-day rule on the crisis team whiteboard.
Hand the monthly check to the team's lead nurse.

pitfalls: Long therapy waits → record 'on waiting list' separately and report it.
Therapy delivered by schools or charities is not in the record → ask families at review and record it.
Small numbers → pool teams or extend to 6 months.
Prescribers feel blamed for service gaps → frame it as a capacity measure.
pearls: Recruit a CAMHS psychiatrist and the psychological therapies lead.
Agree what counts as therapy before cycle 1 (named, structured therapy).
Present both prescribing and waiting-list data.
Make the field part of the prescribing template so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Transfers are few → collect over 12 months and keep a running list.
Two services with different records → get access to both before cycle 1.
Arguments over who is the named worker → the protocol should say who by default.
Young people disengage before transfer → record them separately.
pearls: Recruit one CAMHS and one adult team manager.
Invite a young person with lived experience to comment on the form.
Start with a list of all 17.5-year-olds on the CAMHS caseload.
Hand the list to the transition lead to keep it current.

pitfalls: Behaviour plans are held by care providers → ask providers for a copy and record where it is kept.
Out-of-date plans → define 'current' as dated in the last 12 months.
Few psychologists → accept plans from trained care-provider staff.
Overlap with other STOMP audits → state clearly that this measures the plan only.
pearls: Recruit the team psychologist or positive behaviour support lead.
Use the STOMP register as the sampling frame.
Send a standard letter to providers asking for the current plan.
Keep the field in the review template so it is checked at every review.

pitfalls: Few new starts → include the whole trust and 12 months.
Unclear who counts as a specialist → use the MHRA list and agree it with pharmacy.
Inpatient starts at night → allow a second opinion within a set time and audit that time.
Pharmacy block delays treatment → agree an urgent route through the on-call consultant.
pearls: The chief pharmacist is the key ally; they can pull every new start.
Keep a single trust form for the two opinions.
Report men and women separately.
Keep the pharmacy check after the audit ends.

pitfalls: PRN opioids for pain are often forgotten → search the full chart, not just regular items.
Alert fatigue → limit the alert to the benzodiazepine–opioid pair.
Paper charts on some wards → use a pharmacist ward round to find cases.
Addictions teams feel second-guessed → agree the monitoring template with them.
pearls: Recruit a ward pharmacist; they see every chart.
Include Z-drugs and gabapentinoids as a secondary field if the team wants.
Use a simple sedation scale on the observation chart.
Report methadone cases separately because of the 2-week delay in effect.

pitfalls: Few patients on this drug → include every injection over 3–6 months.
Patients leave early → record it as a fail and note the reason.
Home visits cannot meet the rule → flag any home injection as a safety incident.
Timings recorded loosely → the timed sheet fixes this.
pearls: Recruit the depot clinic lead nurse.
Book a 3-hour clinic slot for each injection.
Give patients a leaflet about the observation and not driving that day.
Keep the sheet in the depot procedure.

pitfalls: Out-of-hours admissions when pharmacies are closed → allow a 'withhold until confirmed' plan and record it.
Patient report alone used → count it as a fail.
Few cases → pool all adult wards over 6 months.
Double supply risk if community prescription not cancelled → include this field.
pearls: Recruit the dual diagnosis lead and a ward pharmacist.
Keep a list of local pharmacy opening hours and the out-of-hours addictions contact.
Build the section into the clerking template, not a separate form.
Ask the pharmacist to check the section on the next working day.

pitfalls: Maternity records are in a different system → ask the maternity mental health midwife to check receipt.
Plans made late → track 32 weeks as the deadline.
Small numbers → allow 6–12 months.
Different templates across teams → agree one before cycle 1.
pearls: Recruit the specialist mental health midwife.
Use a caseload list with due dates.
Ask maternity to flag the plan on the booking record.
Make the distribution list automatic.

pitfalls: Duration of underweight hard to find → accept the date of first recorded low BMI.
DXA requested by GP or endocrinology → search radiology and GP letters.
'Consider' is soft wording → the pass counts a reasoned decision either way.
Few patients in adult services → include CAMHS with the 1-year rule.
pearls: Recruit the service's physical health lead or dietitian.
Agree the underweight definition before cycle 1.
Explain results to patients as NG69 advises.
Keep the template line to maintain the change.

pitfalls: Services discharge to GP after diagnosis → the GP or dementia adviser can be the named person; agree this before cycle 1.
Letters have a team phone number only → a team number without a name is a fail.
Dementia adviser services run by charities → include them as coordinators.
Letter templates owned by admin staff → involve the admin lead.
pearls: Recruit the memory service lead nurse.
Check both the patient and GP letters.
Use the dementia adviser service as the default coordinator where available.
Make the box mandatory in the template.

pitfalls: Plans exist in care plans but not in letters → the pass is in the letter sent to the GP.
Warning signs written for one pole only → require both.
Few discharges → pool teams over 6 months.
Template changes need IT time → start with a Word template if needed.
pearls: Recruit a consultant and a care coordinator from one team.
Ask a GP for feedback on the new section.
Reuse the relapse signature from the care plan.
Keep the section in the letter template.

pitfalls: Placements managed by commissioners → agree data sharing before cycle 1.
Reviews done by phone and not written → ask for review reports.
Small numbers → include all current placements.
No designated reviewer → name one as part of the change.
pearls: Recruit the rehabilitation consultant and the placement commissioner.
Use the tracker to show time spent out of area.
Share results with families.
Keep the tracker with the team manager.

pitfalls: Urine not obtained before antibiotics in sick infants → record 'attempted, not obtained' separately so the team is not penalised for correct treatment-first care.
Parent-reported fever without a measured temperature → decide before cycle 1 whether to include (NG143 treats parental report as valid); keep the same rule in cycle 2.
Tests sent but sample rejected or clotted → count as sent, and report rejection rate as a secondary finding.
Order set bypassed by locum staff → build it into the triage prompt, not just the paediatric menu.
pearls: Recruit an ED paediatric nurse lead; most omissions happen before the paediatrician arrives.
Agree with the lab that urine from under-3-month infants is always cultured, not just dipped.
Run a weekly list from ED triage of age <90 days to capture cases as they happen.
Hand the order set and audit spreadsheet to the next rotation's audit lead at changeover.

pitfalls: Amber features not recorded at all → report traffic-light completion as a secondary measure; do not guess features.
Verbal advice given but not written down → the fix makes the record quick; accept a tick plus leaflet name as evidence.
Staff see a mandatory field as box-ticking → pair it with the printed leaflet so the tick produces something for the family.
Seasonal case mix changes between cycles → compare like-for-like months where possible.
pearls: Recruit the ED paediatric consultant and the PAU nurse lead before cycle 1.
Use the Trust or regional fever leaflet already approved; do not write a new one.
Check re-attendance within 7 days as a balancing measure.
Include translated leaflet versions to cover families with limited English.

pitfalls: Saturations recorded only after oxygen started → use the triage and first ward readings; mark 'unknown' rather than guess.
Night-time dips and probe artefact → define 'persistent' before cycle 1 (for example 2 readings 15 minutes apart).
Nurses worry about lower targets → share the NICE 2021 rationale and the trial data on readmission.
Small numbers outside winter → collect over the season peak.
pearls: Recruit the ward sister and a respiratory nurse; nurses start and wean oxygen.
Record length of stay and readmission within 7 days as balancing measures.
Agree the 'underlying condition' exclusion list at the start.
Keep the chart change in the winter surge plan so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Trial of salbutamol in older infants with wheeze → agree before cycle 1 whether a documented single trial in over-12-month infants counts as a fail; keep the rule fixed.
Diagnosis coded as bronchiolitis but clinically viral wheeze → exclude only if the notes state the alternative diagnosis.
ED doses before admission → include ED drug records, as that is where most doses are given.
Pop-up fatigue → alert only on the listed drugs, not all nebulisers.
pearls: Include the ED team; most salbutamol is given before the ward.
Share each case of a listed drug with the prescriber anonymously in feedback.
Pair with a parent leaflet explaining why inhalers are not used.
Report results with the winter pressures data so managers see the length-of-stay link.

pitfalls: Small numbers → use 24 months retrospectively and report counts, not only percentages.
Fluid start time missing (ED bolus not timed) → take the first recorded IV fluid time from ED notes; mark 'unknown' if absent.
ED and ward teams blame each other → include both in the feedback and the change.
Pump users not disconnected → record as a secondary item, not a pass criterion.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric diabetes nurse specialist as co-lead; they see every DKA case.
Use the BSPED calculator print-out as the data sheet; it already has times.
Case-review any episode with cerebral oedema alongside the audit.
Leave a simple case log so the next trainee can re-audit without searching coding.

pitfalls: Stop time of IV insulin not recorded → use the infusion chart end time; mark unknown if missing.
Transition timed with a meal and done out of hours by agency staff → include the step in the nursing section, not only medical notes.
Pump users managed by family → record the time the family restarted the pump.
Small numbers → report counts and each failure as a case story.
pearls: The diabetes nurse specialist is the natural co-lead.
Link to the fluid–insulin timing audit so one data pass covers both.
Ask the ward pharmacist to check overlap on the EPMA at the ward round.
Store the case list in the diabetes team folder for the next cycle.

pitfalls: Decision time not recorded → agree to use prescription time; note it underestimates delay.
Postnatal ward babies wait for a neonatal doctor to cannulate → capture cause of delay to target the right fix.
Babies on the NNU skew results → report postnatal ward and NNU separately.
Grab bags not restocked → assign a named band 5 nurse per shift.
pearls: Co-lead with a neonatal nurse or ANNP; they give most first doses.
Run a 'mock sepsis' drill on the postnatal ward in week 4.
Display monthly median time on the NNU safety board.
Agree grab-bag restocking with pharmacy before launch.

pitfalls: Culture result not visible at 36 hours → measure lab reporting time too; NICE 1.16.1 supports a 36-hour culture result system.
'Strong suspicion' is subjective → agree a local definition (for example red flag or two or more non-red-flag indicators) before cycle 1.
CRP repeat taken late → record CRP timing as a secondary item.
Seniors override the stop date → reasons are captured; review them at the stewardship meeting.
pearls: Recruit the neonatal pharmacist and a microbiologist.
Use the Kaiser or local EOS calculator result as a secondary descriptor, not a pass criterion.
Report bed-days saved; it wins management support.
Keep the stop-date default in the EPMA build, so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: Clinicians unaware of the 2026 change → brief consultants before cycle 1; this is a new recommendation.
Amoxicillin dose for neonates under BNFC review → agree a local dose with pharmacy and microbiology first.
Few eligible babies in small units → combine with a neighbouring unit or extend the window.
Home discharge concerns → start with in-hospital oral switch only; add home care later.
pearls: Co-lead with the neonatal pharmacist.
Record days of IV cannula use saved as a family-centred outcome.
Ask the network to share the template so results can be compared.
Put the eligibility field on the ward-round template so it survives staff change.

pitfalls: Glucose from a gas taken 2 hours earlier → define 'immediately before' as ≤30 minutes before the LP and keep it fixed.
LP time not recorded → use CSF sample receipt minus transport time only if agreed; otherwise mark unknown.
Traumatic or failed LPs → include; the glucose is still needed.
Low numbers in small units → extend the window to 12 months.
pearls: Stick the sticker on the LP pack itself.
Ask biochemistry to flag CSF glucose results without a paired blood glucose.
Include ED and children's ward LPs, not just the NNU.
Record the secondary 4-hour CSF result time to engage the lab.

pitfalls: Time jaundice first noticed poorly recorded → use the first midwifery entry mentioning jaundice; record 'unknown' otherwise.
Transcutaneous reading used first → CG98 requires serum under 24 hours; count TcB alone as a fail and report separately.
Night-time phlebotomy delay → capture who took the sample.
Few cases → extend to 12 months if needed.
pearls: Co-lead with a postnatal ward midwife.
Add a laminated flowchart at the TcB meter storage point.
Share each missed case at the maternity safety huddle.
Ask the lab to prioritise bilirubin on babies under 24 hours.

pitfalls: Blood group of mother not requested because 'already known' → count as done only if the result is in the record.
Blood spot result not visible to hospital staff → agree access to the child health record before cycle 1.
Babies seen by midwives in the community → include only hospital clinic attendances in both cycles.
DAT not needed in some units' local policy → keep to NICE and note any agreed local variation.
pearls: Include a stool colour card; it doubles as parent education.
Recruit the clinic nurse or phlebotomist who runs the session.
Track time to specialist referral for any conjugated bilirubin >25 µmol/L.
Keep the proforma in the clinic template library, not a personal folder.

pitfalls: Few eligible babies in a local neonatal unit → use 12 months and consider joining with a network NICU.
Babies transferred in after 72 hours → exclude; record transfers separately.
Ventilated babies with delayed start by choice → record documented clinical reason; decide before cycle 1 whether a documented reason counts as a pass.
Order set not updated in the EPMA build → involve the pharmacy EPMA lead early.
pearls: The neonatal pharmacist can build the order set in a week.
Look at caffeine stopping at 33–35 weeks (NICE 1.3.6) as a second measure.
Present hours-to-caffeine as a run chart.
Use BadgerNet reports so the next trainee can repeat it in an hour.

pitfalls: Point-prevalence counts the same baby repeatedly → report both baby-days and unique babies.
Babies near term with different targets → agree the corrected age cut-off (for example until ROP risk ends) before cycle 1.
Alarm limits changed by staff for comfort → record but do not make them a pass criterion in cycle 1.
Auditor presence changes behaviour → vary the audit days and times.
pearls: Pair a trainee with a neonatal nurse champion for cot-side checks.
Photograph (without patient identifiers) examples of good charts for teaching.
Include ROP screening staff; they support tight targets.
Put the default in the EPMA build so it outlasts the rotation.

pitfalls: Scan requested but family did not attend → count as a fail for the pathway but record DNA separately.
Culture-negative 'UTIs' treated empirically → include only culture-confirmed cases.
Radiology waiting list beyond 6 weeks → share data with radiology; the fix may be a booking slot.
Re-audit too early → allow 6 weeks follow-up after the last case.
pearls: Recruit a paediatric radiographer or sonographer lead.
Use microbiology reports to find cases rather than coding.
Also check DMSA and MCUG against tables 4–6 as secondary measures.
Build the imaging check into the virtual results clinic.

pitfalls: ECG done but not filed → search the ECG system as well as notes.
QTc not calculated by machine for young children → ask cardiology for a manual QTc protocol.
Febrile seizures included by mistake → apply the afebrile rule at case selection.
Clinic sees children already ECG'd in ED → count any ECG before clinic as a pass.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric epilepsy nurse and Epilepsy12 lead; ECG is also an Epilepsy12 measure.
Put an ECG machine in the PAU so it is not borrowed from adult ED.
Teach nurses to record ECGs in children at induction.
Report any abnormal QTc found as a case study.

pitfalls: Plan exists in the epilepsy nurse file but not the notes → check epilepsy nurse records before marking a fail.
First presentation with status where recurrence risk unclear → accept a documented decision that no plan is needed.
Small numbers → extend to 12 months and report counts.
Template not used by ward doctors → have the epilepsy nurse review all admissions weekly.
pearls: Co-lead with the paediatric epilepsy nurse specialist.
Use the regional or BPNA plan format families already know.
Check the rescue dose matches current weight.
Link plan issue to Epilepsy12 reporting.

pitfalls: Discussion held but not written down → the letter heading fixes this; do not accept verbal assurance in cycle 1.
Clinicians feel SUDEP talk is harmful at diagnosis → agree timing (within 6 months) and use NICE wording on individual risk.
Children with absence epilepsy only → keep them in; risk is low but discussion is still expected.
Letters dictated late → use clinic date, not letter date.
pearls: Invite the epilepsy nurse to lead the first discussion, with a leaflet.
Use a short script agreed by the team.
Track Epilepsy12 measures alongside so the change counts twice.
Place the heading in the shared template so all consultants use it.

pitfalls: Girls started by tertiary neurology → count them; the local team shares responsibility for the annual review.
Pre-pubertal girls seen as out of scope → MHRA covers girls; agree this before cycle 1.
Form completed but not scanned → check with the epilepsy nurse before marking a fail.
Second specialist unavailable → set up a buddy consultant for countersigning.
pearls: The register is the fix; the audit then becomes a quarterly check.
Pharmacy can supply the prescribing list in a day.
Include transition-age girls moving to adult services.
Share results with GP practices, which also hold ARAF duties.

pitfalls: Surgical patients under a different team → include both medical and surgical wards; report separately.
Point-of-care gas sodium used instead of lab → NICE says laboratory tests; count gas as a fail in cycle 1 but record it.
Fluids running at low 'keep vein open' rates → exclude KVO fluids explicitly.
Blood draws are distressing → coordinate with other planned bloods; note this in feedback.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric pharmacist and the surgical ward sister.
Link to the NPSA hyponatraemia alert in teaching.
Report lowest sodium as a harm measure.
Put the field in the EPMA build so it outlasts the rotation.

pitfalls: Anaphylaxis coded as allergic reaction → search adrenaline administration records, not only diagnosis codes.
Referral left to GP → NICE says offer referral; accept a documented GP referral request only if agreed locally before cycle 1.
Drug-allergy cases where the drug is easy to avoid → auto-injector criterion does not apply; mark N/A.
Low numbers → extend window to 12 months.
pearls: Recruit the paediatric allergy nurse; they want the referrals.
Stock training pens in ED.
Include adolescents seen in adult ED.
Link the bundle to the Resuscitation Council anaphylaxis algorithm poster.

pitfalls: Small numbers → use 24 months and report each missed case.
HBIG ordered late from UKHSA → record HBIG order date; the Green Book allows HBIG up to 7 days but aims for the same time as vaccine.
Vaccine given but time not recorded → count as unknown, not a pass.
Mother's status unknown at delivery → include and record whether an urgent HBsAg test was done.
pearls: Co-lead with the antenatal screening coordinator.
Keep vaccine stock in the delivery suite fridge.
Notify GP and health visitor for the 4-week and 12-month doses and dried blood spot test.
Review with the UKHSA health protection team annually.

pitfalls: Unwell babies deferred appropriately → accept a documented clinical reason reviewed by a consultant as a pass; decide before cycle 1.
Vaccine stock not held on the unit → arrange pharmacy supply first.
Babies discharged just before day 56 → exclude; they fall to primary care.
Schedule changes (for example 2025–2026 changes) → use the schedule in force on the due date.
pearls: Recruit the neonatal discharge coordinator.
Put the due date on the cot card.
Tell parents the date at the 2-week update.
Check the red book is filled so the GP does not repeat doses.

pitfalls: Birth time and BG time from different systems with clock drift → check POCT meter clocks before cycle 1.
Risk factors missed at birth → report risk identification as a secondary item.
Babies tested at 1 hour 'to be safe' → share the framework rationale (normal physiological dip).
Midwife workload at night → keep the chart box simple.
pearls: Co-lead with a postnatal ward midwife and the infant feeding lead.
POCT middleware gives exact BG times; ask the POCT team for the download.
Pair with feeding support measures from the same framework.
Report term NNU admissions as the outcome that matters to managers.

pitfalls: Consultant review not time-stamped → the template field fixes this; in cycle 1 use the note time and mark 'untimed' separately.
Night admissions reviewed at a morning ward round after 14 hours → analyse by admission hour to support rota discussions.
Registrar reviews on behalf of consultants → only count staff on the consultant rota, as RCPCH defines.
Short-stay discharges by registrars → record separately (standard 4 covers them).
pearls: Involve the clinical director early; the fix may be rota change, not documentation.
Include weekends in both cycles.
Plot hours-to-review by admission hour.
Share results with the RCPCH regional lead as part of Facing the Future benchmarking.

pitfalls: Aspirin issued by the GP is invisible in hospital notes → agree access to the shared care record or GP summary before cycle 1.
Moderate-risk women muddy the denominator → audit high-risk women only; run moderate risk as a second cycle.
Staff tick the field but no prescription follows → count a prescription, not a tick, as a pass.
Some units prescribe 150 mg, others 75 mg → accept 75–150 mg; record the dose to show variation.
pearls: Recruit the digital midwife early; the EPR change is the fix.
Agree the 16-week cut-off with the lead obstetrician before cycle 1 and keep it for cycle 2.
Ask community pharmacy leads to confirm aspirin cannot be bought over the counter for this use, and put this in the leaflet.
Hand over the dashboard metric to the antenatal clinic matron before rotation.

pitfalls: Numbers fall as fewer units start methyldopa → extend the look-back to 12 months if needed.
Methyldopa still on the discharge letter even when stopped on the ward → record both; the letter drives GP repeats.
Physicians object to switching when blood pressure is stable → the order set allows a documented reason to override.
Paper charts in some areas → check both systems during the pilot week.
pearls: Ask the maternity pharmacist to run the list of methyldopa administrations; it saves hours.
Measure hours from birth, not calendar days, and fix the definition before cycle 1.
Link the change to the postnatal depression screen so midwives see the point.
Give the order set a named owner in pharmacy so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: CO monitors missing in community bags → check monitor stock and calibration with the team lead before cycle 1.
36-week contacts done by phone → record setting; exclude remote contacts from the denominator only if the template allows no CO.
Mandatory field filled with '0' to get past it → spot-check 10 records against the monitor log.
Gains fade after the audit → put the rate on the monthly dashboard.
pearls: Recruit a community midwife champion; most 36-week contacts are in the community.
Agree the 35+0 to 37+6 window before cycle 1.
Pair the audit with the tobacco dependence adviser so positive readings reach treatment.
Use the same EPR report for both cycles.

pitfalls: Numbers are small → use 12 months per cycle and report counts, not only percentages.
Steroids given at another unit before transfer → check transfer letters.
Clinicians object that some births cannot be predicted → report 'no opportunity' cases separately.
Definitions drift between cycles → fix 'full course' as two doses 24 hours apart.
pearls: Pull the list from the neonatal dataset, which already records steroid status.
Recruit a neonatal registrar; steroid timing matters to them too.
Present each case as a short timeline; it drives change better than a rate.
Combine with the magnesium audit to share one data pull.

pitfalls: Very small numbers → audit 12–24 months and present each missed case.
Infusion started but not charted → check the infusion chart and anaesthetic record.
Precipitate births skew the rate → record 'no opportunity' cases separately.
Toxicity worries → include the monitoring chart in the pack.
pearls: Neonatal data already hold this field; ask the neonatal data clerk.
Recruit a labour ward coordinator to own the preterm box.
Agree how to count births within 1 hour of arrival before cycle 1.
Use a simulation drill to launch the box.

pitfalls: Timing not recorded → count missing time as a fail and fix the form first.
Neonatal team worry about delaying resuscitation → include clamping with the cord intact or resuscitation at the bedside as passes where available.
Late preterm births outnumber very preterm → report by gestation band.
Caesarean births recorded in a separate system → check both.
pearls: Recruit a neonatal consultant and an anaesthetist; clamping happens between teams.
Agree what counts as 'documented reason' before cycle 1.
Use the theatre team brief to say 'deferred clamping planned' out loud.
Report monthly to keep the gain.

pitfalls: Diagnosis uncertain (no pooling, test used) → include only women managed as preterm rupture of membranes by the team.
Antibiotics continued at home without a stop date → check the discharge prescription.
Stewardship team may prefer another agent locally → agree the standard with them before cycle 1.
Small numbers → extend to 12 months.
pearls: Recruit the maternity pharmacist and microbiologist early.
Use a 10-day auto-stop, not a reminder.
Count co-amoxiclav separately; it is the headline safety issue.
Give the order set to the triage lead to own.

pitfalls: Results reported after booking never reach the notes → check the lab system against the EPR alert for every case.
Rapid births give no chance → report 'birth within 1 hour of arrival' separately.
Penicillin allergy labels vary → record the agent used.
Home-birth women with GBS → include only if they laboured in hospital.
pearls: Ask microbiology for a list of positive antenatal results; it is the easiest denominator.
Agree the alert wording with the digital midwife.
Show neonatal colleagues the babies who needed 36 hours of observation because antibiotics were missed.
Hand the monthly report to the labour ward manager.

pitfalls: Antibiotic time and incision time on different clocks → use the theatre system time for both where possible.
Category 1 births make timing hard → report them apart; still count them.
Antibiotic given but not charted → check the anaesthetic chart and drug record.
Anaesthetists see this as their domain → run the audit jointly with the obstetric anaesthesia lead.
pearls: Recruit an obstetric anaesthetist as co-lead.
Agree the data source for incision time before cycle 1.
Keep the checklist line short so it gets said aloud.
Feed results into the surgical site infection surveillance programme.

pitfalls: Decision time written from memory later → take it from the call sheet or emergency bleep time.
Staff feel blamed → present delays as system causes (theatre busy, anaesthetist elsewhere).
Category misclassified (category 2 labelled 1) → record the indication and check against the NICE definition.
Small numbers → pool 6 months.
pearls: Recruit the labour ward coordinator; they hold the times.
Agree 'decision time' is the time the obstetrician states the category aloud.
Report the median and the longest times, not only the pass rate.
Link cases to neonatal outcome for context.

pitfalls: Carbetocin not on formulary or in stock → confirm with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Cost objection → show NICE's cost-effectiveness rationale and the extra oxytocin infusions avoided.
Pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease need care → accept a documented reason as a pass.
Uterotonic recorded only as 'given' → count missing drug name as a fail.
pearls: Recruit the lead obstetric anaesthetist and the theatre pharmacist.
Change the tray, not only the guideline.
Record blood loss to show safety.
Keep the pre-printed chart line after rotation.

pitfalls: Last dose time unclear with continuous epidurals → use the time the infusion or top-up stopped.
Checked but not written → the chart box fixes this; spot-check.
Women transferred to the ward before 4 hours → the due time must move with the handover.
Night shifts miss checks → report results by time of day.
pearls: Recruit a postnatal ward midwife champion and the obstetric anaesthesia lead.
Agree 'last dose' definition before cycle 1.
Put the due time on the handover sheet, not only the chart.
Audit a small monthly sample to keep the gain.

pitfalls: No PGD, so midwives wait for a doctor → set up the PGD before cycle 2.
Contraindications not recorded → the required line includes a 'contraindicated' option.
Pre-eclampsia and haemorrhage cases → count as passes only if documented.
Birth-centre births recorded on paper → include them.
pearls: Recruit a senior midwife from the birth centre and labour ward.
Ask pharmacy to prepare the PGD early; it takes weeks.
Ask women about pain at the first postnatal check to show impact.
Keep the required line after rotation.

pitfalls: Small numbers → take 12 months.
Laxative on the ward chart but not on discharge → check both.
Grade recorded differently in theatre and birth records → use the operation note.
Local protocol differs on agent → accept any laxative; record which.
pearls: Recruit the perineal specialist midwife; they hold a case list.
Build the order set with the maternity pharmacist.
Add the follow-up clinic booking to the same order set.
Report with the antibiotic rate for a fuller picture.

pitfalls: Telephone contacts counted as visits → count face-to-face only.
Weekend discharges drive delay → report by discharge day.
Discharge time not recorded → use the EPR discharge timestamp.
Staffing pressure blamed → show the delay pattern to support a rota change.
pearls: Recruit the community matron.
Agree the clock start (discharge timestamp) before cycle 1.
Break results down by locality and day of week.
Keep the worklist field after the audit.

pitfalls: Tests done in primary care not visible → confirm the pathology system shows GP requests before cycle 1.
Letters change but tests do not follow → measure both the letter and the test.
Re-audit too soon to see tests → re-audit letters at week 13, tests at 6 months.
OGTT still used by some practices → record it; it is a fail against the standard.
pearls: Recruit the diabetes specialist midwife and a GP lead.
Pull the cohort from the diabetes clinic list.
Put the due date in the letter, not only 'at 6 weeks'.
Link to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme referral.

pitfalls: Mifepristone not stocked in the unit → confirm supply with pharmacy before cycle 1.
Two visits needed → offer home misoprostol where local policy allows.
Incomplete and missed miscarriage mixed → use the scan report to classify.
Surgical rates are the real outcome → record them for context.
pearls: Recruit the early pregnancy unit lead nurse.
Ask pharmacy for a monthly issue list of mifepristone.
Include the 3-week pregnancy test in the pack (rec 1.11.7).
Keep the pack after rotation by naming an owner.

pitfalls: Gestation by dates used instead of scan → take gestation from the scan report.
Older guideline copies in circulation → remove them from the unit and intranet.
Blood bank issues anti-D on request without checking → involve the transfusion practitioner.
Small numbers of RhD-negative women → take 6 months.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner; the blood bank log is the fastest data source.
Audit only cases after the 2026 update date.
Show the number of unnecessary doses avoided.
Update the patient leaflet at the same time.

pitfalls: Previous miscarriage history not asked → the template prompt makes it a required question.
GPs decline to continue prescribing → agree shared care with the ICB before cycle 2.
Wrong preparation or dose → record the product used.
Started before intrauterine location confirmed → count as a fail.
pearls: Recruit the early pregnancy unit lead and the ICB pharmacist.
Agree the 'eligible' definition with the scan report wording.
Include the continuation plan in every GP letter.
Keep the prompt in the template after rotation.

pitfalls: Results from primary care not visible → confirm the pathology system shows GP requests.
Test done but anaemia not treated → the template asks about iron too.
Advice-and-guidance referrals missed → include them if seen in clinic.
Unneeded hormone tests continue → record them as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the gynaecology outpatient lead and a GP referral lead.
Agree the 3-month window before cycle 1.
Offer iron at the first visit to show benefit to patients.
Keep the template field after rotation.

pitfalls: Few cases → search 24 months of coding and letters.
Coding is poor → also search letters for 'premature ovarian insufficiency' and 'premature menopause'.
Second FSH done by the GP → check the pathology system for GP requests.
AMH used as a shortcut → record it as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the menopause or reproductive medicine lead.
Ask the lab for a list of patients under 40 with raised FSH to cross-check.
Put the checklist in the letter template, not a separate form.
Pair with a bone health check as a later cycle.

pitfalls: Scan waiting lists are long → report time to scan as well as whether it was done.
Women who have never had sex may decline transvaginal scan → accept an offered-and-declined record.
Radiology capacity objection → agree the extra demand with radiology before cycle 2.
Mixed referral reasons → define 'suspected endometriosis' by referral wording.
pearls: Recruit a sonographer and the gynaecology triage consultant.
Agree the referral form change with primary care leads.
Show the number of endometriomas found to justify capacity.
Keep the triage rule written in the referral guidance.

pitfalls: No same-day fitter → record referrals and time to fitting; fix access alongside.
'Offered' ticked without discussion → spot-check free-text notes.
Pharmacy and online EC outside the audit → state the setting clearly.
Fitting rates stay low even when offered → report offer and uptake separately.
pearls: Recruit a senior nurse fitter to hold emergency coil slots.
Agree what counts as 'not appropriate' before cycle 1.
Offer a leaflet comparing EC methods.
Keep the field after the audit.

pitfalls: Recall visits after NAAT results often skip culture → the hard stop is at the treatment step.
Transport delays make cultures fail → record lab failures separately.
Pharyngeal sites missed → count each positive site.
Nurses and doctors use different templates → change both.
pearls: Recruit the lead health adviser and the microbiologist.
Check culture positivity rates too; a taken swab that never grows is a lab issue.
Agree the site-by-site pass rule before cycle 1.
Link to test-of-cure decisions under the 2025 guideline.

pitfalls: Follow-up takes 6 months, so re-audit must wait → plan the re-audit date at the start.
People tested elsewhere → check shared lab results.
Recall numbers out of date → confirm contact details at treatment.
People living with HIV followed in HIV clinic → include HIV clinic results.
pearls: Recruit the lead health adviser; they run recalls.
Record the treatment titre too; without it the 6-month result means little.
Use the same look-back window in both cycles.
Keep the automatic recall owned by the EPR administrator.

pitfalls: Prescribing rules still settling locally → agree the local doxyPEP protocol before cycle 1.
Online and postal prescriptions use another system → include both routes.
People living with HIV counted as fails → mark them as 'not applicable, pass'.
Template fatigue → keep fields to single clicks.
pearls: Recruit the PrEP lead nurse.
Audit the other BASHH measures from the same records for little extra effort.
Agree definitions with the health adviser team.
Keep the template owned by the service manager.

pitfalls: Source HIV status unknown and poorly recorded → the proforma asks for source group.
Starter packs issued without notes → cross-check the pharmacy issue log.
ED staff see it as a sexual health task → run it jointly with the sexual health lead.
Follow-up loss → record the referral as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit an emergency medicine consultant and a sexual health consultant.
Use the pharmacy log to find every starter pack.
Agree what counts as 'consider' before cycle 1.
Keep the proforma linked to the sexual health referral.

pitfalls: Active bleeding is hard to judge from notes → agree a simple definition (drop in Hb with visible bleeding or haemodynamic instability) before cycle 1.
Blood bank issues two units at once for convenience → agree with the lab that the second unit is issued only on request.
Clinicians object in low-weight or very anaemic patients → allow a documented reason as a pass.
Small numbers on one ward → pool across the hospital.
Order-set change delayed by IT → use a paper sticker on the prescription in the interim.
pearls: Recruit the hospital transfusion practitioner early; they already have issue data.
Report 'units saved' alongside compliance; it persuades managers.
Pair with the Hb threshold field so you do not double count threshold audits.
Hand the dashboard to the transfusion team so it survives your rotation.

pitfalls: Haematology day-unit patients go home before a count → accept a count at next attendance if documented plan.
Doses are recorded as bags not adult doses → confirm dose conversion with blood bank.
Pre-procedure transfusions often skip the count → note procedure type separately.
Order-set change needs IT time → start with a printed sticker.
pearls: The transfusion practitioner can pull issue and count data in one report.
Present the cost per platelet dose; it gets attention.
Flag low-bleeding-risk procedures (NG24 1.7.8) as a secondary finding for a later cycle.

pitfalls: Transfusion in theatre is missed by ward doctors → pull cases from LIMS, not notes.
IT will not auto-populate → a free-text heading still works.
Donation wording seen as irrelevant in older patients → keep it; it is part of the standard.
Gains fade after rotation → make the heading mandatory.
pearls: The transfusion practitioner can send the list weekly.
Ask the GP practice liaison for one example of a missed transfusion; it makes the case.
Keep the fixed text short: one line per item.

pitfalls: Review happens verbally on rounds but is not written → count only written decisions and say so.
Weekend starts miss the window → record day of start and analyse separately.
Prompt fatigue if the pop-up fires daily → set it once at 48 hours.
Definitions drift between cycles → fix the 48–72 hour window in advance.
pearls: Partner with the AMS pharmacist; they already run point-prevalence sweeps.
Use the Start Smart Then Focus five decisions as the drop-down list.
Feed back ward-level results; competition helps.

pitfalls: Specialist letters say 'continue' without a review → accept only if dated in last 6 months.
Patients object to stopping acne antibiotics → offer a topical plan at review.
Search misses acute issues repeated manually → search issues, not only templates.
Gains fade → the review date on the template is the lasting fix.
pearls: Recruit the PCN clinical pharmacist; this is squarely their work.
Run the search before and after with the same saved report.
Report the number of antibiotic courses avoided.

pitfalls: Patients cannot recall the date → accept year or 'childhood' and pre-agree this.
Mandatory fields invite 'unknown' → audit the rate of 'unknown' separately.
IT change takes months → use pharmacy reconciliation to complete fields meanwhile.
Old allergy imports from primary care lack detail → count them but analyse separately.
pearls: Ward pharmacists can complete the data and the fix; recruit them.
Show one real near-miss where 'penicillin' meant nausea; it lands well.
Use penicillin labels as the seed for a de-labelling project.

pitfalls: Hospital shared-care letters override GP templates → check both.
Mixed 2.5 mg and 10 mg strengths → record as a secondary safety flag.
Prescribers write 'weekly' and think it enough → the standard needs the day.
Template edits lost when a new strength is added → recheck at re-audit.
pearls: Practice pharmacists can fix templates in an afternoon.
Ask community pharmacy to report prescriptions without a day.
The same search works for weekly oral bisphosphonates.

pitfalls: Remote appointments skip the questionnaire → send it electronically before the call.
Nurse-led clinics use a different form → include all prescribers in the template.
Clinicians see PROMs as box-ticking → agree an action pathway for high scores.
National guidance may change again → note the version used in each cycle.
pearls: Recruit the acne nurse specialist; they see most follow-ups.
Use the same PROM at every visit so change can be tracked.
Share results with the BAD audit lead to avoid duplicate work.

pitfalls: Out-of-hours and hospital starts are not captured → note the source and include only practice starts.
Clinicians see the template as extra clicks → keep it to four fields.
Short courses under 7 days inflate pass rates → record days' supply.
Codeine co-preparations are missed by searches → include combination products.
pearls: Use the TARGET-style patient leaflet in the template.
The PCN pharmacist can run the search each month.
Track 'on repeat at 3 months' as the outcome that matters.

pitfalls: Re-audit window is long → pick a sample started right after the change and look back at week 13–14 or extend to 20 weeks.
Hospital-started statins have no practice recall → include them and code the source.
Patients do not attend → count a recall sent plus two reminders as a separate measure.
Changing the definition of 'change' between cycles → fix it in advance (drug or dose).
pearls: Recruit the practice phlebotomy lead to pre-book the blood test at initiation.
Report the proportion reaching >40% non-HDL reduction as a bonus outcome.
Use one saved search for both cycles.

pitfalls: HBPM values held in free text → search both codes and free text.
Monitor shortage → a loan scheme or pharmacy BP check service solves it.
Clinicians code 'raised BP' then 'hypertension' later → use the first hypertension code date.
Small practices may have few cases → pool across the PCN.
pearls: Recruit the healthcare assistants who fit ABPM.
Report how many were not hypertensive after ABPM; it justifies the time.
Use a standard HBPM diary with average calculation.

pitfalls: Heart failure is under-coded → also search for loop diuretics plus echo letters.
Hospital cardiology may have stopped it → accept a documented reason.
Genital infection and DKA concerns → include sick-day advice as a field.
Supply problems change practice → note any shortage.
pearls: The practice pharmacist can do most of the reviews.
Start with HFrEF, where evidence is strongest, then widen.
Pair with the eGFR field so renal limits are checked.

pitfalls: QRISK done in primary care is not visible → check the summary care record.
Dermatologists feel CV risk is the GP's job → the GP letter paragraph shares the load.
Phototherapy lists are nurse-led → include nurses in the proforma change.
Very young patients have low scores → still counts as assessed.
pearls: QRISK3 has a free online calculator; build the link into the proforma.
Nurse specialists can record it at the monitoring visit.
Report the number with QRISK ≥10% not on a statin.

pitfalls: Few starts per month → look back 12 months for cycle 1.
Aspirin bought over the counter is not on the chart → check clinic letters.
Thrombocytopenia contraindicates aspirin → record platelet count.
Protocol change needs pharmacy approval → involve the chemo pharmacist early.
pearls: The haematology pharmacist can pull all IMiD starts in one report.
Record VTE events as an outcome; it strengthens the case.
Align with the local myeloma protocol wording.

pitfalls: The review happens in primary care and is not visible → check GP records via shared care record.
Provoked status is never recorded → make it a field at diagnosis.
Re-audit window is long → sample diagnoses from the first 2 weeks after the change.
Haematology capacity for clinics → a virtual or GP template works.
pearls: Recruit the anticoagulation nurse; they often run the DVT clinic.
Use the HAS-BLED field for unprovoked cases as a quality marker.
Report days of anticoagulation avoided.

pitfalls: Nurses dipstick by habit at triage → the triage protocol must change, not just doctors' practice.
Clinicians fear missing sepsis → emphasise symptom-based assessment and culture.
Dipstick results are not always recorded → check obs charts and ask the ward.
Fit, community-dwelling women over 65 may use the under-65 tool → record and analyse separately.
pearls: Recruit the ED nurse educator and the AMS pharmacist.
Remove dipsticks from resus/triage trolleys for the pilot.
Count antibiotic courses avoided.

pitfalls: eConsult and phone contacts have no exam → record contact type and analyse separately.
Locums do not use the template → include in locum pack.
Winter peaks change case mix → keep the same season if possible.
Coding varies (URTI vs sore throat) → fix the code list in advance.
pearls: Pharmacy First handles many sore throats; include their referrals in context.
Auto-scoring templates cut the effort to one click per item.
Report antibiotic prescription rate by score band.

pitfalls: Local SOP still demands eGFR for everyone → update the SOP with the radiology lead first.
Radiographers ask verbally and do not record → add the checklist to the RIS.
Measuring over-testing and under-assessment together confuses the message → keep pass criterion single; report delays as secondary.
GP requests come by paper → include the questions on the paper form.
pearls: Recruit the CT superintendent radiographer.
Report scans delayed or cancelled for bloods; it shows the benefit.
Use the NICE wording verbatim on the form.

pitfalls: Receipt date is not the discharge date → use workflow receipt date.
Reconciliation is done but not coded → agree one code in advance.
Pharmacist leave stalls the queue → set a cover rule.
Summaries arrive without medicines → exclude and report separately to the trust.
pearls: The practice pharmacist is the natural owner.
Report discrepancies found; it proves value.
Feed poor-quality summaries back to the trust.

pitfalls: Cancer flag missing on requests → check the pathway via the cancer tracker as well.
Outsourced reports have different timestamps → confirm which field is 'final'.
Weekends inflate calendar days → report working days too.
Radiologist workload objection → show the numbers are small.
pearls: Recruit the RIS manager to pull timestamps in bulk.
Cancer MDT coordinators know which scans were FDS.
Present time lost per patient against the 28-day standard.

pitfalls: ICU staff are not all entitled operators → check the entitlement list with the RPS first.
Evaluation made verbally on the round → only written entries count.
Radiology reports quickly in some units → exclude films reported before line use.
Sticker not stocked → keep it in the CVC packs.
pearls: Work with the radiation protection supervisor; this fills their audit requirement.
Put the box on the existing CVC insertion sticker, not a new form.
Same method works for NG tube and chest drain films.

pitfalls: The 50–79 thresholds are below the old 35 → results between old and new cut-offs are the ones most likely missed; flag them.
Ultrasound done privately or elsewhere → check shared record.
Lab comment change needs pathology approval → involve the duty biochemist early.
Some women are symptomatic of another cause → note documented alternative diagnosis.
pearls: Recruit the clinical biochemist; the lab comment is the lasting fix.
The ICB cancer GP lead can circulate results.
Count cancers found in the 'new threshold' band.

pitfalls: SFLC costs more → agree with the lab that lab add-on is cheaper than delayed diagnosis.
Many SPEP requests are not for myeloma → use clinical details to classify.
Urine samples never arrive → the serum test set removes this problem.
Test set not used by all practices → check uptake by practice.
pearls: The clinical biochemist can build the test set and add-on rule.
Report time to diagnosis for any myeloma found.
Share practice-level uptake with the ICB.

pitfalls: Migraine is under-coded or coded as 'headache' → search both codes and confirm the diagnosis in the notes before including
Clinicians say the triptan or NSAID was contraindicated → record contraindications and report opioid use with and without them
Opioids given before the diagnosis was made → record the time of diagnosis and count only doses given for the migraine
Pushback that patients 'expect' strong analgesia → share the NICE wording and the medication overuse risk, and include re-attendance as a balancing measure
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a neurology or headache nurse as joint leads
Ask pharmacy to run the opioid report for migraine diagnoses; it takes minutes
Give patients a one-page migraine discharge leaflet with triptan advice and medication overuse warning
Track re-attendance within 7 days to show that the change is safe

pitfalls: Letters say 'uses painkillers frequently' without a number → count only a days-per-month figure as a pass
Consultants use personal templates → agree one shared template line at the department meeting before cycle 2
Referral letters lack the information → add the question to the GP referral form as well
pearls: Ask patients to bring a headache diary to the first visit; the clinic letter invitation can request it
Recruit the headache specialist nurse to champion the template line
Report how many patients met the overuse threshold; it shows the value of asking

pitfalls: The decision date is unclear in letters → agree before cycle 1 that it is the clinic date when the person agreed to start
Deferred starts inflate delays → record patient-chosen deferral separately and exclude it from the pass rate
Infusion-unit capacity sits outside the MS team → invite the day-unit manager to the results meeting
Small numbers per drug → report overall and by route, not by individual drug
pearls: Recruit the MS nurse or treatment coordinator as co-lead; they hold most of the dates
Chart each step (bloods, funding, homecare, dose) to show where the weeks go
Request screening bloods at the diagnosis visit when treatment is likely
Share the result with the homecare provider; their set-up time is often the longest step

pitfalls: Acknowledgement is clicked without action → count a pass only when an action or plan is recorded.
Reports on GP patients sit outside the EPR → include GP-referred cases and ask the practice or use the ICE/GP results log.
Alert codes applied inconsistently by reporters → agree the code list with radiologists before cycle 1 and keep it fixed.
Escalation emails go to a generic inbox → route them to named leads and the results coordinator.
pearls: Recruit the RIS manager early; most systems can export alert and acknowledgement times.
Show two or three real delayed cases (anonymised) at governance; they move people more than percentages.
Give the results coordinator ownership of the monthly figure so it survives trainee rotation.

pitfalls: Outsourced reporters use a different template → agree the field with the teleradiology provider before cycle 1.
Calls made but written only on paper → accept the EPR or report addendum only, and say so in advance.
Radiologists see it as extra typing → make the field a short pick-list plus a name box.
Small numbers in one month → pool 2 months if fewer than 40 alerts.
pearls: Recruit a consultant radiologist who chairs the discrepancy meeting as co-lead.
Also record minutes from report to call; it is a useful secondary measure.
Ask the PACS team to build a monthly report of CRITICAL alerts without a named receiver.

pitfalls: Personal mobile numbers entered → count only numbers that switch with the rota.
Pre-filled numbers go out of date at changeover → give switchboard ownership of the list.
Checking numbers is slow → test a random 10 by phone, not all 50.
IT change takes months → use a hard-stop free-text field as an interim step.
pearls: Ask radiologists how many calls failed last week; it wins support quickly.
Agree what counts as 'valid' with the radiology lead before cycle 1.
Include night requests; that is where the gap usually is.

pitfalls: Weekend reports wait until Monday → include weekend days in the rota slot or the 72 hours will fail.
Reviews done but not recorded → count only EPR sign-off or a written note.
Radiology and ED disagree on what is 'abnormal' → use the radiology alert or discrepancy code as the definition.
Work-list grows at busy times → report backlog size weekly to the ED lead.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant who already does results review; they know the pain points.
Record patient contact outcome; it supports Duty of Candour reporting.
Keep the work-list slot in the rota, not in a person's goodwill, so it survives rotation.

pitfalls: GP results out of hours cannot be phoned → agree the out-of-hours GP route before cycle 1 and count calls to it.
Call time not typed into the LIMS → make the call record a required step to release the comment.
Different thresholds for renal patients → list agreed exceptions in advance and exclude them in both cycles.
Lab staff feel blamed → present the data as a system measure with the biochemistry lead.
pearls: Recruit the duty biochemist and a senior biomedical scientist.
Report time to call by hour of day; night-time delays usually show a staffing issue.
Use the same 2026 limits in both cycles.

pitfalls: Microbiology phones the consultant's secretary → count only calls to a clinician in the last team.
Discharge time missing in the LIMS → pull it from PAS.
Contaminants inflate the denominator → agree the contaminant list before cycle 1.
Ward teams have rotated → use the team bleep, not an individual.
pearls: Recruit a microbiology registrar; they make these calls.
Record what happened to the patient; recalled cases make a strong governance story.
Ask the ED to name one clinician per shift as the results contact.

pitfalls: Denominator is small if you use only positives → count all sets taken, not just positive ones.
Definition of contaminant drifts between cycles → fix the organism list with microbiology before cycle 1.
Packs not restocked at night → give ownership to the ED stock manager.
Teaching alone fades → rely on the pack and feedback rather than sessions.
pearls: Recruit a microbiologist and an ED nurse educator together.
Show the cost and extra antibiotic days per contaminated set.
Feed back rates by shift or area monthly; it keeps the change alive.

pitfalls: Second set delays antibiotics → state that both sets can be taken in one draw, as SMI S 12 allows, and antibiotics must not wait.
Lab counts bottles, not sets → agree how the LIMS shows a set before cycle 1.
Contamination may rise with more sets → track contamination as a balancing measure.
Order set change needs IT time → start with a printed two-label pack.
pearls: Pair with the contamination audit; both use the same LIMS extract.
Recruit an ED sepsis nurse lead.
Show single-set cases later labelled 'possible contaminant' to explain why two sets matter.

pitfalls: Collection time missing or defaulted to label print time → report missing times separately and fix the label workflow.
Hub-and-spoke labs blame transport → split delays into collection-to-receipt and receipt-to-load.
Capital cost of a new module → start with courier timing, which is cheaper.
Seasonal volume changes → re-audit in the same season if possible.
pearls: Recruit the microbiology laboratory manager; they own the analyser log.
Plot delays by hour of collection; the night peak is usually obvious.
Use the same week-day pattern in both cycles.

pitfalls: Free-text search misses nodules → search several terms and check a sample of chest CTs by hand.
Reports do not state size → ask radiologists to use the BTS size bands in the code.
Respiratory team fears extra workload → show that most small nodules are discharged by the MDT, not seen in clinic.
Follow-up requested but never done → record whether the CT happened as a secondary measure.
pearls: Recruit the lung nodule MDT lead and a chest radiologist.
Fix the size cut-offs to the BTS guideline in both cycles.
Give the nodule nurse the tracking list; it survives trainee rotation.

pitfalls: Emergency scans cannot wait for fluids → accept a documented 'not given: emergency' as a pass.
Clinicians argue the evidence is weak → NICE says 'consider', so the pass is a documented decision, not fluid itself.
eGFR from months earlier → use the latest eGFR before the scan and state this rule in advance.
Heart failure patients → record the reason; do not push fluids.
pearls: Recruit a renal registrar and a CT vetting radiologist.
Report AKI after scans as a secondary measure; it keeps the audit balanced.
Keep the prompt short; a one-line pick list is used, a paragraph is not.

pitfalls: Mandatory fields invite ticking 'no' without asking → compare the request answers with the radiographer's full screen.
Unconscious patients cannot answer → allow 'unknown: collateral being sought' and record who is chasing.
IT change is slow → use a required free-text line as an interim.
MRI staff and referrers blame each other → present the data jointly with the MR safety expert.
pearls: Recruit the MR safety expert and a senior MRI radiographer.
Measure delays caused by safety queries; they show the cost.
Keep the question list identical in both cycles.

pitfalls: Mixing stroke and trauma protocols → filter by clinical indication, not protocol name alone.
Repeat series inflate DLP → record them separately so the protocol is judged fairly.
One scanner drives the result → report per scanner.
Re-education alone gives small gains → change the protocol, not only behaviour.
pearls: Recruit the medical physics expert first; they can pull dose data quickly.
Use the NDRL version adopted in 2022 in both cycles.
Check image quality with a neuroradiologist after any protocol change.

pitfalls: Out-of-hours radiographers unfamiliar with gating → include night scans and give them a one-page set-up card.
Fast or irregular heart rates → record the reason when gating is not possible and accept it as a documented exception.
Series names vary by scanner → agree how gating is identified with the CT superintendent before cycle 1.
Small numbers → pool 3 months.
pearls: Recruit a cardiothoracic or vascular radiologist and the CT superintendent.
Report motion artefact as a secondary measure; it shows why gating matters.
Make the gated protocol the default so it survives staff turnover.

pitfalls: Lock-out blocks a doctor during an emergency → keep a short-term emergency ID that is audited weekly.
Training capacity cannot meet demand → agree extra training sessions with the POCT team before the lock-out date.
Doctors rotating in without training → add POCT training to ED induction.
Middleware data unfamiliar to clinicians → ask the POCT coordinator to run the extract.
pearls: Recruit the POCT coordinator; they own the register and middleware.
Announce the lock-out date early and publish weekly counts of expired users.
Keep the same analysers in both cycles.

pitfalls: Tests done but not documented → count only what is in the record; say so in advance.
Batch number seen as bureaucracy → share the MHRA recall case study.
Kits in several places → put them in one place next to the EPR terminal.
Paper and electronic records mixed → check both in cycle 1 and cycle 2.
pearls: Recruit an ED senior nurse and the POCT coordinator.
Use the same age band and exclusion rules in both cycles.
Stick the batch number label on the kit box to make copying easy.
